Therefore, turning away from what has now become, as it were, a sacrilegious usage and custom, we have judged that religion should be provided for to this extent: that the parish be governed in turn by priests placed outside it. For those who live there have learned to kill their shepherds with the sword, and by an unheard-of crime (one that has never happened anywhere at all, even in provinces afflicted by continual and varied incursions of war) this city has been found which, without persecution, strikes down the prelates who minister the Christian faith to it. Care must therefore be taken that this deadly pestilence there be healed by the suspension of bishops of its own, and so at least the fuel of such great fury be withdrawn; and in this way that city, having no one on whom to rage, may either desist because of this suspension, or may not offer its dreadful contagion to others to imitate. Contend for justice for your soul, and strive for justice even to death, and God will fight down your enemies for you. Do not be hasty in your tongue, and useless and slack in your works. fixed.author: SS Bonifacius II
fixed.before: Through our son Armenius, priest and abbot, we have received the letter of your fraternity, which, as it seems, you had sent to us while still unaware of the priestly office entrusted to me, in that charity by which we are bound in God; in it you had thought it right to ask that what you had requested of our predecessor of blessed memory, Pope Felix, for the strengthening of the catholic faith, should be carried through by my urging. But since the will on high has so disposed that what you had hoped to obtain from him through us you should rather obtain from us, we have not delayed to give a catholic reply to your petition, which you conceived out of praiseworthy concern. For you report that some bishops of the Gauls, while they now agree that the other goods come from the grace of God, would have faith alone, by which we believe in Christ, to be of nature, not of grace; and that it has remained in the free will of men from Adam, which it is wicked to say, and is not also now conferred on individuals by the bounty of divine mercy. You ask that, to remove the ambiguity, we should confirm by the authority of the apostolic see your confession, in which you, on the contrary, define, in accordance with catholic truth, that right faith in Christ and the beginning of all good will is inspired in the minds of individuals by the prevenient grace of God. And so, since many Fathers, and above the rest Bishop Augustine of blessed memory, and also our forebears the prelates of the apostolic see, are shown to have discussed this matter so very fully and with reason that it ought to be doubtful to no one any longer that faith itself also comes to us from grace, we have thought it right to refrain from a lengthy reply; above all since, according to those sentences which you have cited from the Apostle, where he says: 'I have obtained mercy, so that I might be faithful' (I Cor. VII); and elsewhere: 'To you it has been given for Christ's sake, not only that you believe in him, but also that you suffer for him' (Philip. I), it plainly appears that the faith by which we believe in Christ, like all good things, comes to individual men from the gift of grace on high, not from the power of human nature. We rejoice that your fraternity too, having held a conference with certain bishops of the Gauls, has judged this in accordance with the catholic faith: namely in those points in which, as you have reported, they defined with one consent that the faith by which we believe in Christ is conferred by the prevenient grace of the Godhead; rejecting also [the idea that there is] anything at all good according to God which anyone can either will, or begin, or perform, or complete without the grace of God, since our Saviour himself says: 'Without me you can do nothing.' For it is certain and catholic that in all good things, of which praise is the chief, divine mercy goes before us while we are still unwilling, so that we may will; is present in us when we will; and follows also so that we may endure in faith; as the prophet David says: 'My God, his mercy shall go before me' (Psal. LVIII); and again: 'My mercy is with him' (Psal. LXXXVIII); and elsewhere: 'His mercy shall follow me' (Psal. XXII). Likewise blessed Paul says: 'Or who has first given to him, and it shall be repaid to him? For from him and through him and in him are all things' (Rom. XI). Hence we greatly wonder at those who think otherwise, that they are still so weighed down by the remnants of the ancient error as to believe that one comes to Christ not by the gift of God but by nature; and that they say the good of nature itself, which is known to have been corrupted by Adam's sin, is the author of our faith rather than Christ; and do not understand that they are protesting against the Lord's sentence, which says: 'No one comes to me unless it has been given to him by my Father' (John VI); and are at the same time also opposing blessed Paul, who cries out to the Hebrews: 'Let us run to the contest set before us, looking to Jesus Christ, the author and finisher of faith' (Hebr. XII). This being so, we cannot find what they attribute to the human will, without the grace of God, for believing in Christ, since Christ is the author and finisher of faith. Therefore, greeting you with fitting affection, we approve your confession written above as consonant with the catholic rules of the Fathers. As for those who, as you report, would attribute the other [goods] to grace while faith comes first, we bind them by their own profession, so that they are compelled far rather to ascribe faith too to the gift of grace, without which there is nothing good that anyone can do according to God, as the blessed Apostle says: 'Everything that is not of faith is sin' (Rom. XIV). This being so, either they will attribute no good to grace, if they strive to withdraw faith from it; or if they say that any good is from grace, faith itself must necessarily be attributed to grace. For if there is nothing good without faith, and yet faith itself is denied to come from grace, then no good, God forbid, will have to be attributed to grace. For the apostle James says: 'Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights' (Jac. I). And they themselves admit, as you say, that the other gifts are given through grace; and they do not doubt that all goods themselves subsist through faith. Faith itself, therefore, must necessarily be attributed to grace, since they cannot separate from it the good which they attribute to grace. These points having thus been briefly set out, we have not thought it necessary to reply to the remaining absurdities of the Pelagian error which that letter seems to contain, which you reported was sent to you by a certain bishop: for we hope from the divine mercy that through the ministry and teaching of your fraternity he will deign so to work in the hearts of all whom you reported as dissenting, that from this they may believe that all good will proceeds not from themselves but from divine grace, when they find that they now wish to defend what they were stubbornly striving to attack. For it is written: 'The will is prepared by the Lord' (Prov. XIX, according to the LXX), and elsewhere: 'I know that I cannot be continent unless God gives [it], and this itself was [a mark] of wisdom, to know whose gift this was' (Wis. VIII). May God keep you safe, dearest brother. Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of February, in the consulship of Lampadius and Orestes, men of senatorial rank (A.D. 530).

fixed.author: SS Bonifacius II
fixed.before: Not relying on unreasonable confidence, nor ignorant of my own mediocrity, but with a contrite soul and a humble spirit, and with many tears, I offer you this my supplication, and I therefore think it acceptable before you, most blessed father: for formerly also those who supplicated God with tears prayed with confidence, as if with burnt offerings and rams and bulls, and indeed with ten thousand fat lambs: for 'God will not despise a contrite and humbled heart' (Psal. L). So neither will you, most holy father, hold me in contempt, surrounded as I am by many evils and looking only to God and, by paternal custom, to your piety. Since no ecclesiastical order can surpass that power of yours which was conferred on you by the Saviour of all and first shepherd, nothing is small or lowly to which your providence looks. The more you surpass all before God, the more you must reflect that this is the proof of those who love God, as Peter, after God the father and leader of the holy Church, testifies to you and to the whole world. For when the Lord said for the third time: 'Do you love me? Feed my sheep' (John XXI), he handed over the commands, showing [them] first to you, and then through you bestowed them on all the holy Churches throughout the whole world. Finally, it is for this reason that those who were made venerable before you, all who were found worthy to hold that holy see, while living in body in the glorious city of Rome, yet in spirit adorned all that was duly done and passed beyond [it]; and very many members of the body of the Church have been set free from the violence of slandering enemies by God and the venerable apostolic see. Hence I beseech you: judge the humble, and do justice to the poor, as it is written (Psal. LXXXI). For in secular life I formerly held a provincial rank in the service, and I passed my life humbly and modestly, as it was. But when Proclus of blessed memory, who had been made bishop of the Church of Larissa, went to his rest, and a prelate had to be ordained for that Church, a decree was made jointly by the clergy as well as the people, the metropolitan, and those whose assent was necessary for the act; and, according to ancient custom, three were chosen: Alexander, a priest of Sciathos, and ..., a priest, and my lowly self; and having obtained the better testimony I won the palm of election. But I, knowing myself, judged myself unworthy of so great a task; yet I gladly assented to it all by the grace and clemency of God, looking to the thief and the publican and very many other examples of this kind, whom God suddenly snatched from extreme evils and, as one must say, from the very depth of evils; by these I was encouraged, and a certain hope of a good purpose was given me. So all of them conferred the election on me in God, subscribing together to the decree. And since according to ancient custom the ordination had to take place not elsewhere but in the same city, the holy synod of the province assembled, together with the landowners of the whole city and the whole body of the Church, and with the common testimony of all, nothing departing from custom, I was ordained bishop in the church. For Probianus, beloved of God, bishop of the city of Demetrias, showed such eagerness in this matter, and so embraced what had been done, that he even took it upon himself to deliver praise in the Church of God on the person of my humble self. And so that, without my saying anything about myself, it may be understood from those who wanted and elected me that this ordination came about according to God. Therefore I beseech you, most blessed father, to deign to hear these things gently; for I do not put them forward out of love for the praise of my own lips, as it is written, since he who glories in himself cannot be approved before God, but so that, once you know these things, the calumny raised against me may plainly appear to you. How much the bishops of the province and the clergy of the holy Church then said, showing that they rejoiced at my election, I have judged superfluous for your ears. So while the enemy of all good things was quiet, and God did not look upon my sins, the Church suffered no disturbance, and the charity of all was covering offences, as it is written. But, incited from I know not where, Antonius, a God-fearing priest and steward, and Probianus the defamer, bishop of the city of Demetrias (I mean, most blessed one, that same Probianus who, pushing aside others hastening to speak my praises, himself delivered in the church before God the titles of my praise), along with Demetrius, beloved of God, bishop of the city of Sciathos, and persuading others to be partners in their faction, not ashamed of the subscriptions contained in the decree, nor Probianus of his own praise and the testimony of the whole Church, nor of what they had said or done, how they embraced my ordination, how my person had been pleasing to them even before the ordination, how they gladly accepted the ordination once performed, suddenly set out for the imperial city, and, composing a certain accusation, laid complaints before the most holy archbishop of that same city, Epiphanius, saying that my ordination did not at all accord with the holy canons, hoping that another bishop might be substituted in my place. As I begin to speak of these things, distress certainly holds me back. fixed.before: Let us return, then, to that sum in what was said above concerning that year [...], by which you learned that in the first year of the passover celebrated in Egypt the second moon fell on the Kalends of January. If you are willing to attend to it, you will remove this same day most fully. For the aforesaid sum contains 766,625 days. From these deduct 365 days, namely those of the last year of the cycles, so that it may appear that this day too, born of the septenary number from the increase of twelfths, was excluded through this sum. Learn also that the twenty-first moon of the eighty-fourth year is fully bare, without twelfths. And when you restore the aforesaid days to the sum above and divide it, you will find the second moon, which you know was marked on the Kalends of January at the head of the second cycle by the hand of the one who spoke. With these 365 days deducted, then, 766,260 days remain. Divide these by sixty and you will have 12,771; add this to the aforesaid sum, and there will be 779,301 days. Divide these by thirty and you will find 25,967, with 21 days over. These are the twenty-first moon of the eighty-fourth year. When the aforesaid 365 days are restored to that sum above, there will be 766,625 days, as above. Divide these by sixty and you will find 12,777, a twelfth; add this to the aforesaid sum, and you have 709,400 days, a dupondius, a twelfth. Divide these by thirty and you will have 25,980, with a dupondius and a twelfth over, just as the moon is headed at the head of the second cycle; and you will be brought to that same day which we have very often said must be removed at the end of the cycles. Whoever you are, then, wounded by the guile of madness or ignorant of this reckoning, recognise through what high and deep sum of division (or rather, to speak more truly, through what clear demonstration) this day was excluded from the septenary number. If you have been unable to remove a whole [day] in your reckoning, you are found a novice on both counts. Stop, I beg, stop now pressing wretched peoples into error through deceit with your little subversions. Submit your hard necks at last to the truth, which, through mists and illusions, as though coming to you from Egypt, from unknown stretches of provinces and long distances of lands, [comes as] a messenger of the most holy day of Easter, to be celebrated out of season and very often in vain. For when you glue the lunar course of these cycles into the sense of your heart, then you will find a true foundation from the first year of the passover sacrificed in Egypt, which you know to be quite consistent with both the true lunar lattices and the Easter headings. You already know from what was said above that the second moon was found and held at the head of the cycles on the Kalends of January. From those Kalends you will reckon to the day before the same Kalends of January of the following year, and there will be 365 days. To these add the second moon, which fell on those same Kalends, as he said [...], and they make 367 days. Divide these by sixty and you will find six days, a twelfth, two *selae*; add this to the aforesaid sum, and you have 373 days, a twelfth, two *selae*. Divide these by thirty and you will find twelve; there is over thirteen, a twelfth, two *selae*. You must reckon in the same way in the following year, which is called third in order. Twice 365 make 730 days. Put in, as above, the second moon of the first year, and you will have 732 days. Divide these by sixty and you will find twelve; two *selae* remain. Add this to the aforesaid sum and there will be 744 days; two *selae* remain. Divide these by thirty and you will find twenty-four days, with twenty-four over; two *selae* remain. In this way you will reckon each single year up to the eighty-third year; the eighty-fourth you recognise as noted at the end of the cycles. So you will be seen to put in eleven days and a twelfth in each of these years, and you will be known not to have erred at all in the windings of the lattices or in the lunar headings. For our Lord Christ, obeying his Father's command, so brought forth the kindly star of this moon that [...] it might thin the clouds of the darkness of night [...]. Borne on a clear course, free from errors [...], with secret causes at work, it now withdraws when full, to be filled again, and with its revolving courses is bounded once more. These, then, are the beginnings of the moon and its duties, divinely established in perpetual service; these were made foreknowing in signs and in seasons and in days and in years. Through this chaste and pure fabric, and as a foreshadowing of his majesty, the Lord signified with respect to the church that it is very often thinned by various misfortunes and is always diminished in the lapsed, yet, supported by the brightness of its splendour, it grows in the saints. To say it specifically: the church itself speaks thus of itself: 'I am dark,' it says, 'and comely, O daughters of Jerusalem.' And the Lord answered through the Prophet with a sonorous voice, saying: 'You are all beautiful as the sun, and perfect as the moon.' And again: 'Once I have sworn by my holy one, if I lie to David, his seed shall remain for ever, and his throne as the sun in my sight, and as the moon perfect for ever.' This whole mystery remains for the church in Christ and belongs to it. For we most attentively represent the most perfect course of the same moon, so that you may know it to be wholly bounded, in a way, within its lattices on each single day. From the Kalends of January, I say, you will reckon to the day before the day on which you are seeking the moon's age. But perhaps you say: why [reckon] to the day before and indicate the moon's age on the following day? Because you gather the sum from the Kalends of January and put in on top the age the moon had on them. Could you in any way count one day, split in two or doubled, as a single one in the number? So divide these by sixty, and put the result of your division above the number of days. Divide these likewise by thirty, and on any day, as I said, you will most skilfully mark what age the moon will be, [...] through each single day and year. It is true that the birthday of every Easter is generated only by the new day of the first month. But that this first month is commonly said by all to run from the third day before the Nones of March to the fourth day before the Nones of April, let it be shown by sure and ordered reasoning, so that the birth of Easter may be uncovered within these twenty-nine days and shown more clearly through the first annual cycle by true proofs. For from the making of the sun and moon, which took its beginning on the fifth day before the Kalends of April, we reckon that 340 free days ran to the coming fifth day before the Nones of March. To these days we add the fifteenth moon, the fullness in which the moon had been set by the Lord at evening on that same fifth day before the Kalends of April, and they make 355 days. Divide these by sixty, and you have five, eleven-twelfths;

objection.english: who will there be when he accuses [it] truly?

fixed.before: 23. Very well. For whomever it seizes for itself it causes to fall not only into this vice but into many other vices; and at the urging of the ancient enemy himself they become persecutors not only of the Church but also of her priests. objection.english: to accept
objection.explain: Deferre here means to tender or pay the fee: the prohibition covers demanding or offering payment, not demanding or accepting it.

fixed.author: Gregorius I Magnus
fixed.before: 5. Following the ancient rule of the Fathers, I establish that nothing is ever to be received for ordinations, neither for the giving of the pallium, nor for the handing over of documents, nor under the name of *pastellus* [a fee], which a new pretence devised through ambition. For since the pontiff lays his hand on the bishop to be ordained, while the minister reads the Gospel reading and the notary writes the letter of his confirmation, just as it does not befit the pontiff to sell the hand which he lays on, so the minister or notary ought not to sell his voice or his pen at his ordination. For the ordination, the pallium, the documents and the *pastellus* I altogether forbid the one who is to be ordained or has been ordained to give anything. If anyone presumes to demand or to accept anything from these aforesaid things under the name of a fee, he will lie under guilt in the strict judgement of almighty God. But if he who has been ordained, not by agreement, neither pressed nor asked, after receiving the documents and the pallium, wishes to give something to anyone of the clergy solely as a token of thanks, we in no way forbid this to be accepted, because his offering, which did not proceed from the ambition of the receiver, brings no stain of guilt.

objection.explain: The messengers came from the others, not to them: πρός with the genitive marks their origin.

fixed.author: Libanius
fixed.before: And yet many feet carried many people every day to many others, both inviting them and reproaching them for not coming, and this did not make his office any smaller; but if anyone had been sent to me, it would have been cast down at once and trampled underfoot, and would not have been what it was.
fixed.after: And yet every day many feet brought many [messengers] from the others, both inviting him and complaining that he did not come, and this did not make his office any smaller; but if anyone had been sent to me, it would have been cast down at once and trampled underfoot, and would not have been what it was.
fixed.reason: πρός with the genitive is 'from', and the participles agree with τῶν ἄλλων: others sent to the governor, inviting him. The contrast with 'if anyone had been sent to me' survives either way, so the error is minor.

not_upheld.reason: 'The last sea' is what the Vulgate's mare novissimum says, as the Douay version has it; that it means the western sea is the sense of the Hebrew, not the wording of the Latin being translated.

objection.original: τῆς βοηθείας ἢν ἐβοήθησεν αὐτῷ τὴν πρὸς ἐμὲ χάριν αἰτιώμενος
objection.english: had attributed the help that the man gave him to the man's gratitude towards me
objection.explain: The governor said he had helped Julian out of gratitude towards the speaker; the English reverses benefactor and recipient.

not_upheld.reason: The Greek allows either reading, since αὐτῷ can refer to the governor. The English follows the sentence before, in which the man had done the governor a service: the governor credited that service to the man's goodwill towards the speaker, which is why he could not plead ignorance of their friendship.
